summaryEn: Forged aluminium wheels for Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Jaguar Land Rover, made in Yunlin. The operating business is recovering — but the reported quarterly earnings have been swinging on currency, and the FY2025 dividend was larger than the FY2025 profit.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; forged-wheel framing — the premium customer list, lightweighting logic and diversification target credited, with the verified limited US tariff exposure included, but the central data trap made explicit: quarterly results are dominated by FX in both directions (2025Q2's NT$208m valuation loss caused the reported loss while operating profit stayed positive; 2025Q1's 18.5% net margin vs 15.6% operating margin was the mirror image), the FY2025 dividend of NT$2.0 exceeds EPS of NT$1.38, and the 131× P/E is kept and explained as arithmetically correct on TTM EPS of NT$0.45; sector 電機機械 → Forged Aluminium Wheels)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Superalloy Industrial (巧新科技, TWSE: 1563) makes **forged aluminium wheels** — the lightweight, high-strength wheels fitted to performance and luxury cars. Founded in **1994** in Yunlin and admitted to the **Taiwan Stock Exchange main board in May 2024**, it supplies **Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Jaguar Land Rover** and Toyota Tsusho Taiwan, and is one of the few companies anywhere operating at the scale and quality these customers require.

The product distinction matters. Most wheels are **cast** — molten aluminium poured into a mould. Forged wheels are made by **compressing solid aluminium billet under enormous pressure**, aligning the metal's grain structure to produce a wheel that is significantly **lighter and stronger** for the same size. That reduces unsprung mass, which improves handling, ride and efficiency — and it costs far more to make. It is a premium product for premium vehicles, and electrification increases its value because battery weight makes every kilogram elsewhere more expensive.

The recent financial record needs to be read with one specific caution, because the headline numbers are misleading in both directions. **Quarterly results have been dominated by foreign-exchange movements.** In **2025Q2 the company reported a net loss of NT$65m (EPS −NT$0.29) — but its operating profit was still positive**; the loss came mainly from an **FX valuation loss of about NT$208m** on a large foreign-currency position. In **2025Q1 the same mechanism ran the other way**: a **net margin of 18.5% against an operating margin of 15.6%** inflated that quarter's EPS to NT$1.53. Anyone comparing quarterly EPS is measuring the New Taiwan dollar, not the business. **The operating margin is the only reliable series**, and it reads **15.6% → 8.3% → 3.9% → 3.3% → 8.7%** across the last five quarters: a real decline, and a real recovery now under way.

Annual EPS fell from **NT$3.32 (FY2024) to NT$1.38 (FY2025)**, with 2026Q1 at **NT$0.60** and monthly revenue up **6–21%** in recent months. At **NT$57.90 the shares trade at 1.53× book and yield 3.45%** — but the **FY2025 dividend of NT$2.0 exceeded FY2025 EPS of NT$1.38**, a payout above 100%. The reported **P/E of 131.6× is arithmetically correct** on trailing twelve-month EPS of about **NT$0.45**, and is retained on this page for that reason.

Management is diversifying: the target is to lift **non-passenger-car-wheel revenue from 15% to over 40% within three years**, into **semiconductor equipment parts, consumables and aluminium recycling**. On tariffs, the verified position is reassuring — **US shipments are under 15% of revenue**, with only about **5–6% exposed to tariff-rate changes**.

The honest read: **a genuinely differentiated manufacturer with an enviable customer list, recovering operationally, whose reported earnings are so distorted by currency that only the operating line is usable — and which paid out more than it earned.**

Superalloy was founded in **1994** in **Yunlin**, in central Taiwan, to do something Taiwanese manufacturers were not then known for: **forging aluminium to aerospace-grade standards for the automotive industry**.

The difference between forging and casting is the whole business. A cast wheel is made by pouring molten aluminium into a mould — cheap, fast, and adequate for most cars. A **forged** wheel starts as a solid aluminium billet and is **compressed under thousands of tonnes of pressure**, which aligns the metal's internal grain structure along the load paths. The result is a wheel that is **substantially lighter and stronger** than a cast equivalent. It requires enormous presses, precise die design, controlled heat treatment and machining to very tight tolerances — capital and process knowledge that takes years to accumulate and cannot be improvised.

That capability is why the customer list reads the way it does. **Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Jaguar Land Rover** specify forged wheels on performance models, where reducing **unsprung mass** — the weight not supported by the suspension — measurably improves handling, ride quality and efficiency. Qualifying as a wheel supplier to these manufacturers takes years of validation, because a wheel failure is catastrophic. Once qualified, a supplier stays.

Electrification then made the proposition stronger rather than weaker. **Battery packs are heavy**, and every kilogram they add makes weight elsewhere in the vehicle more valuable to remove — so lightweight components command more attention and more content per car, not less.

The company **moved to the Taiwan Stock Exchange main board in May 2024**. It is now applying the same forging and machining competence beyond vehicles — into **semiconductor equipment parts, consumables and aluminium recycling** — with a stated target of raising **non-passenger-car-wheel revenue from 15% to over 40% within three years**. The logic is familiar to several companies in this collection: a specialised process capability is worth more when it serves more than one cyclical industry.

- **1994 (24 June)** — Superalloy Industrial founded in **Yunlin, Taiwan**, to forge aluminium wheels.
- **2000s–2010s** — Qualifies as a forged-wheel supplier to European premium manufacturers; builds press, heat-treatment and machining capacity.
- **2016–2018** — Dividends of **NT$3.0** for three consecutive years.
- **2024 (13 May)** — **Admitted to the Taiwan Stock Exchange main board (1563)**.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS NT$3.32**; Q4 gross margin **27.6%**, operating margin **14.6%**; dividend **NT$2.27**.
- **2025Q1** — Reported **EPS NT$1.53** on a **18.5% net margin against a 15.6% operating margin** — a favourable FX swing inflating the quarter.
- **2025Q2** — Reported **net loss of NT$65m (EPS −NT$0.29)** despite positive operating profit, caused mainly by an **FX valuation loss of about NT$208m**. H1 revenue **NT$3.633bn (−5.1%)**, gross margin **24%**, EPS **NT$1.28**.
- **2025Q3–Q4** — Operating margin bottoms at **3.9%** and **3.3%**; **FY2025 EPS NT$1.38**, down from NT$3.32. Dividend **NT$2.0** — **more than the year's earnings**.
- **2026Q1** — Recovery: **operating margin 8.7%**, gross margin **22.0%**, **EPS NT$0.60**; monthly revenue up **6–21%**. Target set to raise **non-passenger-car-wheel revenue from 15% to over 40% within three years**; **US shipments under 15% of revenue** with only **5–6%** exposed to tariff changes.

Superalloy's accounts contain **one distortion large enough that ignoring it produces the wrong conclusion**.

- **Foreign exchange dominates the reported quarterly results — in both directions.** In **2025Q2** the company reported a **net loss of NT$65m (EPS −NT$0.29)** while **operating profit remained positive**; the loss came mainly from an **FX valuation loss of about NT$208m** on a large foreign-currency position. In **2025Q1** the reverse happened: **net margin 18.5% against operating margin 15.6%**, inflating reported EPS to **NT$1.53**. Comparing those two quarters' EPS measures the New Taiwan dollar, not the company.
- **The operating margin is the usable series.** **14.6% (2024Q4) → 15.6% → 8.3% → 3.9% → 3.3% (2025Q4) → 8.7% (2026Q1)**. That describes a genuine deterioration through 2025 and a genuine recovery now — the honest version of the story that the EPS line obscures.
- **Annual earnings roughly halved.** **FY2024 EPS NT$3.32 → FY2025 NT$1.38.** First-half 2025 revenue was **NT$3.633bn (−5.1%)** with gross profit down **13.8%**, gross margin **24%**, and a **NT$91m customer annual rebate** recognised.
- **The dividend exceeded the earnings.** **NT$2.0 distributed for FY2025 against EPS of NT$1.38** — a payout above **100%**, funded from reserves rather than the year's profit. The **3.45% yield** at NT$57.90 rests on that decision.
- **The P/E of 131.6× is correct, and is kept for that reason.** Trailing twelve-month EPS is about **NT$0.45**, so the multiple is arithmetic, not error. It is retained because it accurately conveys that **the company is barely earning at present** — the same treatment applied to Taiwan Glass elsewhere in this collection.
- **A capital-intensive balance sheet.** **NT$19.9bn of assets** on **NT$8.25bn of equity** — a **58.6% debt ratio**, high but not unusual for heavy forging and machining capacity — with **NT$2.76bn of cash**. **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$168m** exceeded **NT$131m of net income**, which is healthy.
- **Trailing return on equity is 1.15%** — the direct consequence of a year in which earnings nearly disappeared.
- **Recovery is visible in revenue.** Monthly revenue up **+6%, +19%, +21%** in recent months, with **P/B at 1.53×**.

The financing reality: **a leveraged, capital-intensive specialist coming out of a poor year, whose income statement must be read at the operating line — and which chose to pay a dividend larger than its profit.**

**Stance: a genuinely differentiated forged-wheel supplier to Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and JLR, recovering operationally — with reported earnings so FX-distorted that only the operating margin is usable, and a dividend larger than last year's profit.**

The bull case:

1. **A hard-to-replicate process with a customer list to match.** Forging aluminium wheels requires thousand-tonne presses, die design, controlled heat treatment and tight-tolerance machining. Qualification with **Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Jaguar Land Rover** takes years and is rarely reversed — a wheel failure is catastrophic, so suppliers are not swapped casually.
2. **Electrification strengthens the product.** Heavy battery packs make **lightweighting more valuable, not less**; forged wheels reduce unsprung mass, improving handling, ride and range.
3. **The operating recovery is real.** Operating margin **3.3% (2025Q4) → 8.7% (2026Q1)**, gross margin **18.3% → 22.0%**, monthly revenue up **6–21%**, and **operating cash flow exceeding net income**.
4. **Diversification with a specific target.** Non-passenger-car-wheel revenue from **15% to over 40% within three years** — into **semiconductor equipment parts, consumables and aluminium recycling** — reducing dependence on the automotive cycle.
5. **Tariff exposure is limited and verified.** **US shipments under 15% of revenue**, with only about **5–6%** affected by tariff-rate changes and some customers sharing the cost.

The counter-arguments:

- **The reported earnings are unreliable as a guide.** A **NT$208m FX valuation loss** turned a profitable quarter into a reported loss; the prior quarter's EPS was inflated the same way. Only the operating line can be used.
- **Earnings nearly disappeared.** **FY2024 NT$3.32 → FY2025 NT$1.38**, with **ROE at 1.15%** and a **131.6× trailing P/E**.
- **The dividend exceeded earnings.** **NT$2.0 paid against NT$1.38 earned** — not repeatable indefinitely.
- **Leverage and cyclicality together.** A **58.6% debt ratio** against European premium-car demand, which is itself cyclical and currently uneven.

A **recovering-specialist** thesis: a real moat and a real customer list, bought during a weak patch — provided the analysis uses operating margin and ignores reported EPS.

Superalloy sells **forged aluminium components**, overwhelmingly wheels, into markets that pay for lightness:

- **The core product and why it commands a premium.** A **cast** wheel is poured; a **forged** wheel is compressed from solid billet under thousands of tonnes of pressure, aligning the metal's grain along the load paths. The result is **significantly lighter and stronger** at the same dimensions. That reduces **unsprung mass** — the weight the suspension must control — which improves handling, ride comfort and efficiency in a way drivers can feel. Forging costs far more, so it appears on performance and luxury vehicles.
- **The customers.** **Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Jaguar Land Rover** and Toyota Tsusho Taiwan. These are multi-year programme relationships: a wheel is a safety-critical part, validation is extensive, and once a supplier is designed into a model it typically stays for that model's life.
- **Why electrification helps.** Battery packs add several hundred kilograms. That makes every kilogram removed elsewhere more valuable — for range, for handling, for braking — so lightweight components gain content share as vehicles electrify.
- **The cost structure, and the currency exposure.** Aluminium billet is the main input; presses, heat treatment and machining are heavy fixed costs. Sales to European and Japanese customers are largely in foreign currency, which is why the company **carries a large foreign-currency position** — and why an **NT$208m FX valuation swing** can exceed a quarter's operating profit.
- **The diversification plan.** The same forging and precision-machining capability is being directed at **semiconductor equipment parts, consumables and post-consumer aluminium recycling**, with a target of raising **non-passenger-car-wheel revenue from 15% to over 40% within three years**.

The levers are **premium vehicle programme volumes, aluminium costs, factory utilisation and the mix of non-automotive work**. The strength is a genuine process moat serving customers who cannot easily switch. The vulnerability is threefold: **heavy fixed costs meeting cyclical European premium-car demand, a 58.6% debt ratio, and a currency exposure large enough to make the bottom line unreadable in any given quarter.**

Automotive wheels look like a commodity and split sharply once you look at how they are made.

- **Cast versus forged — two industries.** Cast aluminium wheels are high-volume, price-competitive and produced worldwide, including at very large scale in China. **Forged wheels** are a different business: enormous presses, expensive dies, controlled metallurgy, and machining to tight tolerances. The capital and process knowledge required keeps the field small, and the customers are premium manufacturers rather than mass-market ones.
- **Why supplier positions are durable.** A wheel is safety-critical. Validation covers fatigue, impact, corrosion and manufacturing consistency across a model's lifetime, and takes years. Manufacturers do not resource a qualified wheel supplier to save a few percent — which is why **Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and JLR** relationships, once won, persist.
- **The lightweighting trend, and the EV twist.** Vehicle weight reduction has been a steady industry priority for efficiency and emissions. Electrification intensified it: batteries are heavy, and manufacturers compensate by removing mass everywhere else. **Forged wheels are a direct beneficiary** — higher content share per vehicle rather than lower.
- **Where the demand risk sits.** European premium-car production is the dominant driver, and it is cyclical and currently uneven — the same pressure visible in Taiwanese auto-component suppliers such as **Tong Yang (1319)** elsewhere in this collection, though Tong Yang serves the aftermarket and Superalloy serves original equipment.
- **The tariff question, answered.** Verified: **US shipments are under 15% of revenue**, some customers trade on FOB terms, and only about **5–6% of revenue** is exposed to tariff-rate changes, with some customers negotiating cost sharing. This is materially less exposure than the headlines around auto tariffs would suggest.
- **The diversification logic.** Applying forging and precision machining to **semiconductor equipment parts and consumables** targets a customer base with a completely different cycle — a rational response to owning a capability that is not inherently automotive.

Superalloy's position is **strong in a small, technically demanding niche**. The industry truth is that **process capability protects margin but not volume** — the presses still have to be fed, and the orders come from an industry that builds to its own cycle.

**Strengths**
- **Forged aluminium capability** — presses, metallurgy and tight-tolerance machining that few competitors possess.
- **Premium customer base**: **Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Jaguar Land Rover**, Toyota Tsusho Taiwan; multi-year, hard-to-displace programmes.
- **Structural tailwind from electrification** — heavy batteries raise the value of lightweighting.
- **Operating recovery under way**: operating margin **3.3% → 8.7%**, gross margin **18.3% → 22.0%**, monthly revenue **+6% to +21%**; operating cash flow above net income.
- **Limited tariff exposure**: US shipments **under 15%** of revenue, only **5–6%** affected by rate changes.

**Weaknesses**
- **Reported earnings distorted by FX in both directions** — a **NT$208m valuation loss** turned a profitable 2025Q2 into a reported loss.
- **FY2025 EPS NT$1.38 versus FY2024's NT$3.32**; **ROE 1.15%**; trailing **P/E 131.6×**.
- **FY2025 dividend of NT$2.0 exceeded FY2025 EPS of NT$1.38**.
- **58.6% debt ratio** against heavy fixed manufacturing costs.

**Opportunities**
- **Non-passenger-car-wheel revenue from 15% to over 40% in three years** — semiconductor equipment parts, consumables, aluminium recycling.
- Rising forged-wheel content per vehicle as EVs proliferate.
- Recovery in European premium-car production.

**Threats**
- **European premium-car cyclicality** and uneven EV demand.
- **Aluminium price and currency volatility**.
- Fixed-cost leverage amplifying any volume decline.

- **The reported bottom line cannot be used (the most important analytical risk).** **2025Q2 showed a net loss of NT$65m while operating profit was positive**, caused mainly by an **FX valuation loss of about NT$208m**; **2025Q1 showed the mirror image**, with an **18.5% net margin against a 15.6% operating margin**. Any analysis based on quarterly EPS or net margin will reach the wrong conclusion. **Only the operating margin series is reliable.**
- **The dividend exceeded the profit.** **NT$2.0 paid for FY2025 against EPS of NT$1.38.** Paying above 100% of earnings is a signal of confidence in a recovery, but it is drawn from reserves and cannot be sustained if earnings do not recover.
- **Earnings nearly disappeared in 2025.** **FY2024 NT$3.32 → FY2025 NT$1.38**, with **trailing ROE of 1.15%** and a **131.6× P/E** on TTM EPS of about **NT$0.45**. The recovery in 2026Q1 is one quarter old.
- **Fixed costs and leverage together.** A **58.6% debt ratio** funding presses, heat treatment and machining capacity that must be utilised. When premium-car volumes fall, the cost base does not.
- **Concentrated end-market exposure.** European premium and performance vehicles drive demand, and that market is cyclical, currently uneven, and undergoing a difficult electrification transition of its own.
- **Currency exposure is structural, not incidental.** Selling in foreign currency from a New Taiwan dollar cost base creates a position large enough to swamp operating results — and the company has not eliminated it.

Superalloy's outlook depends on **whether the operating recovery holds and whether diversification reduces the automotive dependence.** The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin — and only operating margin.** The series reads **15.6% → 8.3% → 3.9% → 3.3% → 8.7%**. Continued recovery toward the mid-teens would confirm the business is healthy; reported EPS and net margin should be **disregarded** given the FX distortion.
- **The non-automotive share.** The stated target is **15% to over 40% within three years**, into **semiconductor equipment parts, consumables and aluminium recycling**, with meaningful contribution expected from 2026. Progress here structurally reduces cyclicality and is the most important strategic metric.
- **Revenue momentum.** Monthly revenue up **+6%, +19%, +21%** most recently — evidence that premium-vehicle programme volumes are recovering.
- **The dividend.** **NT$2.0 paid against NT$1.38 earned.** Whether the payout is sustained, and whether earnings rise to cover it, will show how confident the board actually is.
- **Currency management.** Whether the company reduces the foreign-currency position that made its 2025 quarterly results unreadable.

Bottom line: Superalloy forges **aluminium wheels for Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Jaguar Land Rover** from Yunlin — a genuine process moat, in a product electrification makes more valuable, with **operating margin recovering from 3.3% to 8.7%**, revenue up **6–21%**, and **limited US tariff exposure (under 15% of shipments, 5–6% rate-exposed)**. It is also a company whose **reported quarterly earnings are dominated by currency swings in both directions**, whose **FY2025 EPS fell to NT$1.38 from NT$3.32**, which **paid a NT$2.0 dividend out of NT$1.38 of profit**, and which carries a **58.6% debt ratio**. Judge it on **operating margin and the non-automotive revenue share** — and never on the reported bottom line.
